passage: Note from Binita, after-school club. At pick-up on Tuesday, Divyansh's father reminded him for the third time to pack his bag the night before. Divyansh rolled his eyes and stared at the wall with his arms crossed. On Wednesday I asked him quietly what that was like. He said, "It's like he thinks I can't remember anything." We practised a sentence he could say instead of sulking or shouting. On Thursday his father began the same reminder and Divyansh answered, "I heard you, Papa. Let me try my way this week." His father paused, then said all right. I will check in with both of them next week.

qa.q: How many times had Divyansh's father reminded him about the bag at pick-up?
qa.a: He reminded him for the third time.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he rolled his eyes?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and underestimated; he said it was like his father thinks he can't remember anything.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do that worked better than sulking or shouting?
qa.a: He said, "I heard you, Papa. Let me try my way this week," which acknowledged his father and asked for room.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's father see the reminders?
qa.a: He probably meant them as care and worry about a forgotten bag, so hearing that Divyansh had heard him helped him step back.

grounding: A child feels lectured by a parent, rolls eyes, then learns to say I heard you and asks to try their own way.
